title: Korean flower piping
subtitle: Buttercream flowers built petal by petal using an Asian-style piping technique
excerpt: Korean flower piping builds flowers on a small nail using a thin, elastic buttercream and a petal tip (number 104 or similar). The petals are thinner and more translucent than classic buttercream roses. Bean paste is traditional; many bakers use Swiss meringue or Italian meringue buttercream for a similar result.
sourceNotes: Korean flower cake decoration became prominent through social media from around 2015 and is associated in large part with the work of Seoul-based cake artists. The technical piping mechanics are adaptations of Western petal-tip work applied to a stiffer, more elastic paste. The approach has been extensively documented in online tutorials and specialist sugarcraft books.

recipe.yieldDescription: One decorative flower arrangement for a 15 to 20 cm cake
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Pipe flowers onto a baking tray lined with baking paper and freeze on the tray for 30 minutes before placing on the cake.

glossaryTerms.definition: A piping tip with a teardrop-shaped opening, one end wide and one narrow. Rotating the bag while piping through a petal tip creates thin, curved petals. Numbers 101, 104, and 123 are the most commonly used in Korean flower piping.

content.text: and a rotating motion to build flowers petal by petal. The buttercream must be stiffer than a spreading consistency: soft enough to pipe without tearing, firm enough that thin petals hold their shape. The kitchen temperature matters more here than in any other decorating technique. Avoid piping above 20 degrees Celsius; at warmer temperatures the petals droop before the flower is finished.

Swiss meringue buttercream or Italian meringue buttercream at around 16 to 18 degrees Celsius pipes the best flowers. American buttercream (icing sugar and butter) is too dense for the fine petals. If the buttercream feels greasy or soft, chill it for 10 minutes in the bowl, then beat briefly before piping. Colour with gel colour, not liquid.
Stick a small square of baking paper to a flower nail or the top of a large piping tip with a dot of buttercream. This is your working surface.
Hold the piping bag at roughly 45 degrees. Place the wide end of the petal tip at the centre, the narrow end pointing up and slightly outward.
Squeeze the bag, rotate the nail slightly with the other hand, and arc the bag in a small fan motion to form the first petal. Release pressure and pull away cleanly.
Add four more petals spaced evenly around the centre, each overlapping the previous slightly.

Slide the baking paper square off the nail and place it on a flat tray. Freeze the flowers for 20 to 30 minutes until firm. Peel each flower from the paper with an icing spatula and place on the frosted cake. The flowers thaw in 10 minutes at room temperature. Add leaves and buds in a contrasting colour to fill the gaps.
